verdicts.note: Live en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tombs_of_Atuan (rendered page + Special:Export wikitext). Quote verbatim: 'making the narrator seem sympathetic to the characters' (cited Cadden 2005 p.92). Both other limbs verbatim too: 'In The Tombs of Atuan, much of the story is told from Tenar's perspective; for instance, the reader sees Tenar's fear of the undertomb through her own eyes, creating an empathy for her' (Cadden 2005 p.94). Minor scope point, not a limb of the claim: the page attributes free indirect discourse to the Earthsea trilogy generally, not to Tombs specifically.

Same page. Verbatim: 'Science fiction writer Jo Walton said that it was a "beautifully written" book. She went on to write that a "lesser writer" would have ended the novel after the earthquake and the collapse of the Tombs, but that the last section of the story, about Ged and Tenar's travel, "do a lot to ground it", making it "solid and well rooted as ever".' Every limb (Walton, final travel section, grounding, after the earthquake) supported.

Live en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehanu. Verbatim: Kirkus Reviews '...even young readers will be beguiled by the flawless, poetic prose, the philosophy expressed in thoughtful, potent metaphor, and the consummately imagined world' (ref Kirkus, January 15, 1990). Both limbs — flawless poetic prose and thoughtful, potent metaphor — supported.

Same page. Verbatim: Dirda in The Washington Post — Tehanu is 'less sheerly exciting' but perhaps 'the most moving'; the book gives the Earthsea themes 'a darker, more realistic edge'; and 'Further, Tehanu presents the world from a woman's point of view...' all carrying ref name 'Dirda 1990' ('The Twilight of an Age of Magic', February 25, 1990). All four limbs supported, and the claim correctly preserves Dirda's 'perhaps'.

Same page. Verbatim: 'Jo Walton finds Tehanu "problematic", writing that it is "a restless book with very strange pacing", but that it is surprising that it "works as well as it does", given the competing demands of "the force of story" - plot, action - and Le Guin's evident intention to place "women's domestic lives" at the novel's centre.' The 'torn between plot and women's domestic lives' limb is supported by that competing-demands sentence; note the page frames it as competing demands the book nonetheless survives, not as a failure.

NEA PDF fetched live (HTTP 200, 515,637 bytes, 12 pages), text extracted with pypdf. Printed page 4, 'The Language of Fantasy': 'Throughout A Wizard of Earthsea Le Guin's language is plain, strong, and exact; her tone grave and slightly formal; and the rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (diction and tone) supported. Page attribution p.4 is correct.
Same sentence, same printed page 4: 'the rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical'. Quote verbatim, limb supported. Page attribution p.4 correct.

Printed page 4, immediately following: 'Note the occasional touches of alliteration and assonance-reminiscent of Old English verse-in such phrases as this: "Forest rises ridge behind ridge to the stone and snow of the heights."' Quote verbatim; the alliteration/assonance limb and the cited example sentence both verbatim. Page attribution p.4 correct.

Printed page 5, 'An Interview with Ursula K. Le Guin': header reads 'On January 7, 2008, Dan Stone of the National Endowment for the Arts interviewed Ursula K. Le Guin at her home in Oregon' - the 2008 limb is confirmed on the page. UKL: 'What a wizard does is like what a writer does. He or she is making things out of words and making things happen with words.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported. Page attribution p.5 correct (the answer sits on p.5, the interview continues onto p.6).

Printed page 9, 'Le Guin and Her Other Works': 'Perhaps the best-known and most taught of all modern science fiction novels, The Left Hand of Darkness is written in a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard of Earthsea.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported. Page attribution p.9 correct.

Printed page 10, Discussion Questions, question 4: 'The language of A Wizard of Earthsea is often quietly poetic. Comment on three sentences that you find particularly beautiful or moving.' Quote verbatim, and it is indeed a discussion question. Page attribution p.10 correct.

Printed page 3, 'Introduction to the Book': 'The book's elegant diction, geographical sweep, and mounting suspense are quite irresistible.' Quote verbatim, all three limbs supported, and it does sit under the heading 'Introduction to the Book'. Page attribution p.3 correct.

verdicts.trueWording: Page credits 'taut and clean' to The Guardian, unnamed
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the attribution of 'taut and clean as a ship's sail' to Craig - the page credits that quotation only to 'The Guardian' and the string 'Craig' does not occur anywhere in the page's HTML (case-insensitive grep of the raw source returned zero hits)
verdicts.note: Live arts.gov page fetched (HTTP 200, 74,952 bytes). Both quotations ARE on the page: the Overview carries '...it is written in prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail.... It poses the deep questions about life, death, power and responsibility that children need answering' (The Guardian), and an accordion panel reproduces the guide's 'Language of Fantasy' text verbatim including 'plain, strong, and exact'. So the 'repeats the guide's characterization' limb and the 'pairs it with' limb are both supported; only the Craig attribution is absent from the page. (Amanda Craig did write the Guardian review, but that cannot be verified from this URL, which is what was cited.)

Live sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/le_guin_ursula_k fetched (HTTP 200, 101,578 bytes). Verbatim: 'The initial Earthsea trilogy, austere but vivid, is a major work whose appeal goes far beyond the Young Adult audience at whom in the first instance it was aimed'. Quote verbatim; all three limbs (austere but vivid, major work, reaching beyond the Young Adult audience) supported.

Same page: 'A grave joyfulness pervades the trilogy, which is perhaps more maturely thoughtful (while remaining exciting) than the comparable Narnia series of C S Lewis.' Quote verbatim and every limb present. FLAG for downstream use: the claim drops SFE's hedge 'perhaps' - the source qualifies the Narnia comparison, so restore 'perhaps' if the sentence is quoted as SFE's position.
